title: Data models and query languages
subtitle: Relational, document and graph models, and how the shape you pick makes some queries easy and others painful.

c.v: This story is made up, but it is a common one.

A small team builds an events app on MongoDB. Each event is one document. Inside it is an array of attendees: user id, name and photo URL. The event page loads with one read. It is fast and the code is simple.
Six months later, three requests arrive in the same sprint.
First, a user changes her name. Her old name still shows on 40 past events. Someone has to write a script that finds and updates every copy.
Second, a big conference sells 30,000 tickets. Its document keeps growing. Every read of the event page now loads all 30,000 attendees.

Third, product wants a page: "events your friends are going to". Users and events now link both ways, and the app has no easy way to ask that question. The team writes code that loads friends, then events, then filters in memory.
Nothing was wrong with MongoDB. The data had changed shape. It started as a tree, one event with its attendees. It became a web of users, events and friendships. The model had not changed with it.

Each model makes some questions cheap and others expensive.

Look at the relationships in your data. If records mostly contain their parts, a document fits. If many records point to many others, tables or a graph fit better. The model decides which queries are easy.

The database's planner compares possible plans and join orders, and picks the cheapest.
When the data changes, it can pick a new plan with no change to your code.
Usually the new plan is better, but not always. A planner can suddenly switch to a slower plan as the data shifts.
So watch the plans of your most important queries.

q.v: Your app shows a blog post with its 20 comments on one screen. Comments are never shown anywhere else. Which model fits this best?

options.v: Embed the comments inside the post document
A graph with a node per comment
Store each comment in its own collection and join on every read

why.v: The post "contains" the comments and they are read together, which is the case MongoDB's docs give for embedding.

q.v: An event document embeds the name of every attendee. A user with tickets to 3 events changes their name. What is the main risk?

options.v: One of the 3 copies is not updated, so the data disagrees

why.v: Denormalised copies must all be updated. If one write fails, the copies disagree.

options.v: The database checks every write against a fixed schema
The code that reads the data decides its structure, and must handle old shapes
There is no structure in the data at all

why.v: The structure is still there, but it is implied. The reader interprets it, so old and new shapes must both be handled.

q.v: You need "all people within 4 hops of this account" for a fraud check. Which query is the most natural fit?

options.v: A Cypher pattern with a quantified relationship like {1,4}
One SQL join with no recursion
A single document lookup by id

why.v: A graph query names a variable number of hops directly. In SQL you need WITH RECURSIVE or several self-joins.

q.v: Why is a declarative query like SQL or Cypher easier for the database to speed up than a hand-written loop?

options.v: It says what result you want, so the database can choose how to get it

why.v: A declarative query states the result, not the steps. The planner is free to pick indexes and join order.
